# On the Strange Gift of Boredom

I've been thinking lately about boredom, that peculiar state we spend so much energy trying to escape. It's the background radiation of modern life—something we're constantly aware of and desperately trying to shield ourselves from. We have phones, streaming services, video games, social media, podcasts for every conceivable interest. We can be entertained at any moment. And yet, if you watch people, especially young people, there's an undercurrent of restlessness. A need to fill every silence, every gap, every moment of potential boredom with something stimulating.

I wonder if we've made a mistake.

Boredom, I think, is badly misunderstood. We treat it like a disease, something to be cured immediately with the next distraction. But I'm coming to believe that boredom might actually be one of the most creative and necessary states a human being can experience.

When you're bored, something interesting happens. Your mind doesn't shut down—it wanders. It makes unexpected connections. It gets restless enough to want something, but not so engaged that it's constrained by the demands of the current task. It's a state of productive dissatisfaction. This is where daydreaming lives. This is where imagination actually originates.

Think about where good ideas come from. People always say they come in the shower, or while walking, or in the moment before sleep. These are all states where your conscious mind isn't heavily engaged in something specific. There's a kind of boredom there—a space where your mind can roam. If you were constantly stimulated, constantly fed new input, would your brain ever have the chance to do this kind of wandering synthesis?

I suspect not.

I read somewhere that the human brain evolved in an environment of extensive boredom. Our ancestors spent a lot of time waiting. Waiting for food, waiting for predators, waiting for the seasons to change. That wasn't a bug in human experience; it was more or less the default state. And in that boredom, our minds developed their unique capacity for imagination, pattern-recognition, and abstract thought. We told stories to ourselves and each other during those boring nights around the fire. We thought about problems. We daydreamed about things that didn't exist yet.

Now we've engineered boredom almost entirely out of our lives, at least for those of us with access to technology. And I'm not sure we've gotten happier. In fact, I'd argue the opposite. There's a kind of anxiety in constant stimulation. Your nervous system is always being activated, always being pulled in new directions. You're never quite satisfied because there's always another thing, another video, another notification. It's a kind of hedonic treadmill, but worse, because the treadmill is moving faster than ever before.

I think about my phone, and how I use it. I have a genuine question in my mind that I want to explore, and instead of sitting with it, turning it over in my head, letting my mind play with it, I immediately reach for my phone. I can Google it. I can get the answer in seconds. Which sounds good in theory. But I've noticed that I don't actually retain these quick answers the way I retain things I've puzzled through myself. And more importantly, I've robbed myself of the boredom period—the time when my mind was actually engaged in productive thinking about the question.

There's something almost meditative about genuine boredom. Not the painful kind, where you're actively suffering and waiting for something. But the kind where you're free and unstructured, with no demands on your attention. You're not doing anything, and nothing is being done to you. You just are. And in that state, something shifts. Your breathing slows. Your mind becomes less anxious. Thoughts arise and fall away naturally.

I wonder if some of the mental health crisis we're experiencing—the anxiety, the depression, the scattered attention—is partly a result of our inability to experience boredom anymore. We've lost access to a state that our minds actually need. We've built a world designed to never let us be bored, and in doing so, we've made ourselves profoundly ill.

The solution isn't to reject technology entirely. That's not realistic, and besides, technology has enormous benefits. But maybe it's to be more intentional about when we use it and when we don't. To schedule boredom, in a sense. To protect pockets of time where we're not consuming anything, not being stimulated by anything, just existing with our own minds.

I've started trying to do this. I'll sit on my porch for twenty minutes without my phone. Not meditating in any formal sense, just sitting. And it's uncomfortable at first. My mind reaches for the phone. I feel slightly anxious without external input. But if I sit with it, something shifts. The anxiety passes. My mind starts to wander. And some of my best thoughts, my best ideas, have come in those quiet periods.

I think the future might belong to people who can tolerate boredom. In a world saturated with information and stimulation, the ability to be unstimulated, to be quiet, to let your mind wander and make unexpected connections—that might actually become a competitive advantage. Not just in creative fields, but in any field where genuine thinking is required.

So I'm making peace with boredom. I'm trying to see it not as a problem to be solved but as a gift to be accepted. A space where my mind can be itself, without the constant demands of the external world. A place where imagination lives.

It turns out, we might have been running from something we desperately need all along.
